clinicalPearls: A subperiosteal collection of blood over a skull bone, confined by the periosteal attachments at the sutures
It does not cross suture lines, in contrast to caput succedaneum and subgaleal haemorrhage
It often becomes apparent hours after birth and enlarges over the first day or two, then resolves over weeks
It is associated with instrumental delivery and may overlie a linear skull fracture in a minority
Resorption of the blood can contribute to jaundice, and a firm rim may calcify as it heals
Management is expectant; the collection should not be aspirated because of infection risk
reference.pathophysiology: A cephalohaematoma forms when shearing forces during birth, often with instrumental delivery, rupture blood vessels beneath the periosteum of a skull bone. Because the periosteum is firmly attached at the suture margins, the accumulating blood is confined to the surface of a single bone and cannot cross the sutures. The collection resorbs gradually; breakdown of the trapped blood adds to the bilirubin load, and organisation at the margins can produce a calcified rim during healing.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from a fluctuant swelling limited by sutures
Skull imaging only if an underlying fracture or intracranial injury is suspected
Assessment for anaemia if the collection is large
Distinguishing it from subgaleal haemorrhage clinically
redFlags: A swelling that crosses sutures and is diffuse, suggesting subgaleal haemorrhage
Signs of significant blood loss or anaemia
Features suggesting depressed or complex skull fracture or intracranial injury
Signs of secondary infection of the collection
reference.prognosis: Cephalohaematoma is usually benign and resolves over weeks to a few months; the main issues are exaggerated jaundice, occasional anaemia and, rarely, calcification or infection.
pitfalls: Confusing it with subgaleal haemorrhage, which is far more dangerous
Aspirating the collection and introducing infection
Missing an underlying skull fracture when clinically indicated
management: Manage expectantly, allowing spontaneous resorption over weeks, and never aspirate the collection because of infection risk
Monitor bilirubin and treat associated hyperbilirubinaemia with phototherapy, escalating to exchange transfusion if severe
Monitor for anaemia when the collection is large
Ensure adequate vitamin K to support coagulation in the newborn
Obtain skull imaging only if an underlying fracture or intracranial injury is suspected, and distinguish clinically from subgaleal haemorrhage
Reassure parents about the slow resolution and possible calcified rim, and escalate if signs of infection, rapid enlargement or neurological compromise appear
